titre: Comte, 1835: the composition of the stars would never be known
accroche: Auguste Comte writes in 1835 that we will never know what the stars are made of. In 1864, Huggins and Miller identify known elements in them.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1835, in the second volume of his *Cours de philosophie positive* (Course in Positive Philosophy), Auguste Comte devotes a lesson to what astronomy can know about the heavenly bodies. It can, he says, determine their shapes, distances, sizes, and motions. Their chemical composition, on the other hand, will remain out of reach, by any means.

## Reasoning, not prejudice

Comte does not say this out of disdain. His argument is clear-cut: of distant bodies, only one sense reaches us, sight. Any question that reduces to visual observations is therefore, he writes, accessible “sooner or later.” Any question that would require another kind of exploration must be dismissed as radically out of reach.

A position, a brightness, a motion can be measured by eye, and so by telescope. But the chemistry of his day is done with samples and reagents, and a star provides none.

He also takes a precaution. It would be rash, he acknowledges, to fix rigorously the limits of our knowledge, and when neither case is clearly visible, one must suspend judgment. Yet for the chemistry of the stars, he rules without hesitation: it is out of reach.

## What the light contained

In 1860, in Heidelberg, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen publish “Chemische Analyse durch Spectralbeobachtungen.” Their principle: a substance heated in a flame and viewed through a prism gives bright lines unique to it. The dark lines that a vapor imprints on light passing through it fall in the same places. The lines of a spectrum thus tell which substances emitted the light, or lay in its path. Bunsen and Kirchhoff thereby discover cesium, announced to the Berlin Academy on May 10, 1860.

Four years later, William Huggins and William Allen Miller point the spectroscope at the stars and compare their lines with those of laboratory elements. For Aldebaran, they find coincidences with sodium, magnesium, hydrogen, calcium, and iron, among others. For Betelgeuse, no line falls on the red hydrogen line, whereas Sirius and Vega show it very clearly. Their conclusion: the stars contain matter identical, at least in part, to that of our system, but they differ from the Sun and from one another in the elements that compose them.

## What gave way

It was not Comte’s logic. His criterion, that what reduces to visual observations is accessible, still holds. What gave way was the hypothesis about what light contains: it carries the chemical signature of what it has passed through. The limit was not in the stars, but in what we knew how to read from a ray of light. Twenty-nine years separate Comte’s sentence from the identifications by Huggins and Miller.

When a discipline declares a certain knowledge off-limits, the useful question is what its signal still contains that the discipline does not know how to read.

quiz.question: On what reasoning did Comte base the impossibility of knowing the chemical composition of the heavenly bodies?
choix: The stars are too far away for their light to arrive in sufficient quantity
Only sight reaches the heavenly bodies, and chemistry requires something other than visual observations
The chemistry of the stars would be of no interest to astronomy, which deals with motions
No instrument of his day could measure such high temperatures
quiz.explication: For Comte, only sight links the observer to the heavenly bodies: what reduces to visual observations is accessible, the rest is excluded. He invokes neither the weakness of the light, nor a lack of interest on astronomy’s part, nor temperature. The error lay in what light contains, not in the logic.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the lines of a spectrum let us read, according to Kirchhoff and Bunsen’s principle?
choix: The distance from the light source to the observer
The number of stars in the source’s galaxy
The age of the light since its emission
The substances that emitted the light or lay in its path
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Each substance has its own lines, bright in emission and dark in absorption: the spectrum signs the composition of the source and of what the light passed through. Here it is not used to read distance, the number of stars, or the age of the light.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Huggins and Miller conclude in 1864 about the composition of the stars?
choix: That they contain elements known on Earth, but differ from one another and from the Sun
That they are all made of the same elements as the Sun, in the same proportions
That they contain no element known on Earth
That nothing can be concluded, since distance makes the method uncertain
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Huggins and Miller find in the stars matter from our system, but note differences from one star to another, for example the absence of the red hydrogen line in Betelgeuse. They judge the method just as reliable despite the distance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Comte propose when a question is neither clearly accessible nor clearly out of reach?
choix: To file it among the accessible questions, pending something better
To declare it out of reach out of caution
To suspend judgment until knowledge advances
To settle it in favor of the simplest hypothesis
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Comte envisions three cases: accessible, radically out of reach, or uncertain, in which case one must suspend judgment. The chemistry of the heavenly bodies, for its part, was placed without reservation in the second.
